title: Speech recognition basics
description: Speech recognition turns audio into text: acoustic model (audio -> phonemes), language model (phoneme sequences -> likely words), now usually one end-to-end neural model (Whisper, Conformer). The pipeline is VAD (voice activity detection) -> features -> decode -> text. Accuracy is measured by word error rate (WER); streaming models return partial results as you speak.
mechanism: VAD gates the recognizer; streaming encoder emits partial hypotheses; final result on endpointing (silence). WER on a representative test set is the metric.
algo: O(audio) streaming; WER is the metric.

title: Wake words
description: Wake words ('hey assistant') gate the microphone: a tiny always-on model listens for the phrase, and only then does the full recognizer engage. The model must be small (runs on DSP), low false-accept (no accidental triggers), and low false-reject (hears you the first time). Training needs thousands of utterances across accents and noise.
mechanism: Tiny keyword-spotting model (DS-CNN) on the always-on DSP; threshold tuned for the false-accept/reject tradeoff; full pipeline engages on trigger. On-device only.
algo: O(audio) tiny model; the tradeoff is the threshold.
demo:
# wake word: tiny always-on gate, full pipeline only on trigger
def keyword_spot(chunk):  # DS-CNN in production; template here
    return b'hey assistant' in chunk

stream = [b'background noise', b'hey assistant', b'what time is it']
for chunk in stream:
    if keyword_spot(chunk):
        print('WAKE: engaging full recognizer (was: DSP-only, microwatts)')
        break
    print('...listening (tiny model, on-device, no audio leaves)')
print('tune the threshold: false accepts annoy, false rejects infuriate')

title: Command grammars
description: Command grammars define what the system understands: fixed phrases ('scroll down', 'go back') compiled into a recognition grammar for maximum accuracy. Grammars beat open dictation for control — the vocabulary is tiny, so accuracy is near-perfect even in noise. The grammar is also the documentation: the help screen lists exactly what you can say.
mechanism: JSGF/SRGS grammar or phrase list; recognizer constrained to the grammar; slots for parameters ('volume <1-10>'). Help = the grammar rendered as sentences.
algo: O(grammar) constrained decode; tiny vocab = high accuracy.

title: NLU intents
description: Beyond fixed grammars, NLU maps free-form utterances to intents + entities: 'dim the lights a bit' -> {intent: set_brightness, level: -20%}. The pipeline is intent classification + slot filling, trained on example utterances. Confidence thresholds decide: high -> act, medium -> confirm, low -> ask. The fallback is always graceful ('I didn't catch that').
mechanism: Intent classifier + entity extractor (small models or LLM); confidence -> act/confirm/ask. Conversation state for follow-ups ('a bit more').
algo: O(utterance) inference; confidence gates the action.

title: Confirmation UX
description: Voice actions need confirmation proportional to their cost: low-cost (scroll) executes immediately; high-cost (delete, send, purchase) confirms ('Delete 3 files?'). The confirmation is itself voice-answerable ('yes'/'cancel'). Undo is the safety net — every destructive voice action is undoable. The rule: the more irreversible, the more explicit the confirm.
mechanism: Cost tiers: trivial (act), reversible (act + announce undo), irreversible (confirm first). Confirmation via voice or tap. Undo window announced.
algo: O(1); the design is the work.
demo:
# confirmation proportional to irreversibility
def execute(action, cost):
    if cost == 'trivial':
        return 'executed: %s' % action
    if cost == 'reversible':
        return 'executed: %s (say "undo" within 10s)' % action
    return 'CONFIRM FIRST: "%s"? say yes/cancel' % action

print(execute('scroll down', 'trivial'))
print(execute('archive email', 'reversible'))
print(execute('delete 3 files', 'irreversible'))
print('rule: the more irreversible, the more explicit the confirm')

title: Noise handling
description: Voice systems live in noise: beamforming (multi-mic arrays focus on the speaker's direction), noise suppression (neural denoisers), and echo cancellation (remove the device's own audio). The recognizer also needs noise-robust training — clean-trained models collapse in cafes. Measure WER in the actual environments, not the lab.
mechanism: Beamform -> AEC (echo cancel) -> neural denoise -> recognizer trained on noisy data. Multi-mic arrays in hardware; single-mic relies on the models.
algo: O(audio) DSP chain; training data decides robustness.
demo:
# echo cancellation: subtract the device's own known output
import math

mic = [math.sin(i*0.5) + 0.3*math.sin(i*2.1) for i in range(20)]  # voice + echo
speaker_out = [0.3*math.sin(i*2.1) for i in range(20)]             # what WE played

cancelled = [m - s for m, s in zip(mic, speaker_out)]
residual = sum(abs(c - math.sin(i*0.5)) for i, c in enumerate(cancelled))
print('residual after AEC: %.3f (voice recovered, own echo removed)' % residual)
print('chain: beamform -> echo cancel -> denoise -> recognizer')
print('train on NOISY data: clean-trained models collapse in cafes')

title: Voice latency
description: Voice latency is the pause between 'stop speaking' and the action: endpointing (detecting end of speech, 300-700ms), recognition, NLU, action. Users perceive >1s as broken. Streaming recognition (partial results during speech) and early endpointing (act on high-confidence partials) cut it. The UI shows listening state so the pause feels intentional.
mechanism: Streaming partials; endpoint on silence OR semantic completion; act on confident partials. Show state (listening/thinking/acting). Budget: <1s end-to-end.
algo: O(1) budget; streaming is the technique.

print('recognition:      150ms (streaming: partials DURING speech)')
print('NLU + action:     200ms')
print('total:           ~650ms')

title: Voice privacy
description: Voice privacy is non-negotiable: the mic indicator is always visible when listening, audio stays on-device unless the user opts into cloud, wake-word processing never leaves the DSP, and recordings are never stored without explicit consent. The architecture proves it — on-device STT (Whisper tiny, Vosk) means there is nothing to leak. Privacy is a feature users choose products for.
mechanism: On-device pipeline by default; cloud only with explicit opt-in; mic indicator OS-enforced; no retention without consent; data minimization (features, not audio, when possible).

title: Offline speech recognition
description: Offline STT runs entirely on-device: Vosk and Whisper.cpp provide full recognition without the network — private, available in tunnels, and free of cloud latency. The models are larger than the wake-word spotter but run on modern phones in real time. Accuracy trails the biggest cloud models, but for command-and-control vocabularies it is more than enough.
mechanism: Quantized models (Whisper.cpp) on CPU/GPU; Vosk's Kaldi models for 20+ languages. Streaming mode for partials. Model download once; updates via app releases.

title: Voice error recovery
description: Voice errors are inevitable — misrecognition, wrong intent, noise. Recovery is designed: show what was heard ('I heard "delete files"'), offer the likely correction, make undo instant, and learn from corrections. The worst design is silent wrong action; the best is transparent + one-step fix. Correction phrases ('no, I said...') are first-class commands.
mechanism: Show the transcript; confirm high-cost; one-step undo; correction commands; log corrections to improve the models. Never silently act on low confidence.
algo: O(1); the UX is the work.
demo:
print('VOICE ERROR RECOVERY PATTERN')
print('1. show what was heard: "I heard: delete files"')
print('2. low confidence -> NEVER silently act (confirm or ask)')
print('3. wrong action -> one-step undo ("undo that")')
print('4. correction is first-class: "no, I said DEFEAT files"')
print('5. log corrections -> improve models')
print('silent wrong action is the unforgivable sin')

title: Voice accessibility
description: Voice control is assistive technology for many: users with motor impairments navigate entirely by voice, so every action in the app must be voice-reachable. That means named controls, full keyboard/voice parity with touch, and no voice-only dead ends (every voice action has a visible/touch equivalent). Test with switch users and voice-control users — they find what checklists miss.
mechanism: Every control named (accessibility label); voice commands map to the same actions as touch; no time-limited voice-only flows. Test with real AT users.

title: Multilingual voice
description: Multilingual voice handles code-switching ('pon la canción shake it off'), accents, and language detection per utterance. The recognizer either runs language ID first or uses a multilingual model (Whisper handles 99 languages). Command grammars need per-language versions; NLU needs per-language training. The hard part is mixed-language utterances — handle them, don't reject them.
mechanism: Language ID per utterance (or multilingual model); per-language grammars/NLU; code-switch-tolerant decoding. Fallback: ask the language.

title: Voice analytics
description: Voice analytics measure what text analytics do: recognition WER per cohort, intent success rate, fallback rate, task completion. The data improves the models — but it is audio, the most sensitive data there is. Aggregate aggressively, retain minimally, never retain without consent. The metrics that matter: did the user get it done without repeating themselves.
mechanism: On-device aggregation where possible; consent-gated retention; WER/intent/task metrics per release. The north star: first-try task completion.
demo:
# on-device aggregation: counts leave, audio never does
from collections import Counter
sessions = [
    {'wer': 0.05, 'intent_ok': True, 'retries': 0},
    {'wer': 0.31, 'intent_ok': False, 'retries': 2},
    {'wer': 0.08, 'intent_ok': True, 'retries': 0},
]
agg = Counter()
for s in sessions:
    agg['sessions'] += 1
    agg['intent_ok'] += s['intent_ok']
    agg['retries'] += s['retries']
print('uploaded aggregate:', dict(agg), '(no audio, no transcripts)')
print('north star: first-try task completion (no repeats)')

title: Voice integration patterns
description: Voice integrates into apps three ways: system-level (the OS voice control drives any app — accessibility), SDK-level (the app embeds STT for its own commands), and assistant-level (deep link intents the assistant can trigger). The right pattern depends on reach: system for accessibility, SDK for custom commands, assistant for hands-free entry points. Most serious apps do all three.
mechanism: System: accessibility labels (free). SDK: embedded recognizer + grammar. Assistant: intent definitions (SiriKit, App Actions) deep-linking into the app.

title: Testing voice systems
description: Voice systems are tested with audio, not clicks: corpora of utterances across accents/noise/devices, WER regression per release, intent accuracy on recorded sessions, and end-to-end task tests ('book a timer' actually sets one). Adversarial tests include accents the training missed and noise profiles from real environments. The test corpus grows with every production failure.
mechanism: Utterance corpora (accent x noise x device); WER + intent gates per release; E2E task tests; production failures -> new test cases. Never ship on lab-audio metrics alone.
algo: O(corpus) per release; the corpus is the asset.
